articles.title: 'We hit it very nicely': Trump confirms US struck Iran's anti-aircraft facility in Qeshm
articles.summary: United States President Donald Trump confirmed that American forces struck an Iranian military facility on Qeshm Island, even as Tehran warned it was
articles.body: United States President Donald Trump confirmed that American forces struck an Iranian military facility on Qeshm Island, even as Tehran warned it was prepared to retaliate and insisted that diplomacy remained possible.The announcement came on Tuesday, as American voters headed to the polls for midterm elections that could weaken Trump's hold on power. The vote has been dominated by public discontent over the war with Iran and the inflation linked to the conflict.Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian warned that a fresh outbreak of fighting would benefit neither side, while senior officials said the country was ready to defend itself if Washington escalated its military action.Trump confirmed the strikes in an interview with Fox News, following several reports that American forces had attacked Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz."They built an anti-aircraft facility... As soon as it was completed, we hit it last night very nicely," Trump said on Fox & Friends, describing the operation as a "minor attack".Iran's state news agency IRNA reported five explosions in quick succession on the island. Some residents also reported seeing two aircraft flying over the area.Asked whether Israel had participated in the latest strikes, an Israeli military spokesperson told AFP, "No".The United States and Israel began their war against Iran with a massive wave of attacks in late February. The conflict has remained largely deadlocked for months.Iranian leaders responded to the latest strikes with warnings of retaliation, while maintaining that Tehran was willing to negotiate.Iran's chief negotiator with the US, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said the Islamic republic was prepared for another round of fighting."The countries of the region should know that, just as the Islamic Republic of Iran stands ready for battle with its finger on the trigger, it has also given the American side a powerful and rational response," he said in a televised address."The ball is now in America's court to prevent war."Iran's deputy foreign minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Iran retained the right to "legitimate self-defence" following the US strikes.Pezeshkian, however, said his government was still seeking to resolve the crisis "through dialogue". He warned that "no one will benefit from this war" if fighting resumed.He also pointed out that Iran's supreme leader had recently given the government additional powers to negotiate issues that had previously been considered "off-limits".The latest exchange came just hours after Trump suggested that an agreement with Tehran remained possible."Iran wants a settlement, as soon as possible," he wrote on Truth Social.Qatar hopeful of interim dealQatar, which has been mediating indirect negotiations between Washington and Tehran, said it remained hopeful that the two sides could reach an interim agreement.Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed Al Ansari said both countries were still engaged in negotiations and that Doha was facilitating the exchange of proposals."Both parties remain committed to the negotiation process; as we mentioned, we are facilitating the real-time exchange of proposals between them," he told reporters.Both sides "are currently reviewing the ideas and proposals we have presented," he added."We remain hopeful that there is still a chance for a deal to take place," he said, adding that Doha was working "towards an interim deal".Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi also confirmed on Monday that indirect negotiations were continuing."Given the sensitivity and gravity of the current situation, consultations and deliberations are very intensive," Araghchi told state media.US Vice President JD Vance said both he and Trump remained optimistic about reaching an agreement."We've certainly made some progress. We'll see if we can make some more," Vance told reporters on Monday.A senior Iranian official said Tehran was prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days, provided Washington accepted its long-standing demands.The strait is a crucial route for global oil and gas shipments. Iran had proposed a seven-day plan in September to reopen it, with conditions that included ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing Iranian assets, lifting oil sanctions and ending the US counter-blockade of Iranian ports."The possibility of implementing this plan in two days is another indication of Iran's good-faith approach," Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said at a briefing.Trump renews threatsDespite the ongoing diplomatic efforts, Trump has continued to threaten further military action against Iran. On Sunday, he said the US might have to give Tehran "the hammer" at an unspecified point.A day earlier, he said he still needed to "take care" of one or two targets, including the so-called Pickaxe Mountain in central Iran. The site is suspected of being linked to Iran's nuclear programme, although Tehran denies that it is a nuclear facility.Iranian officials have repeatedly warned that any resumption of the war would trigger retaliation across the region.The mood in Tehran was reflected in a huge billboard installed in the heart of the capital, AFP journalists reported on Tuesday. Displaying an image of the US president, it carried the message, "We will kill Trump".You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Russia gives its drones bigger antennas to beat Ukraine's jamming
articles.summary: Russia is upgrading its attack drones with larger anti-jamming antennas to counter Ukraine's electronic warfare systems, potentially making it harder for
articles.body: Russia is upgrading its attack drones with larger anti-jamming antennas to counter Ukraine's electronic warfare systems, potentially making it harder for Kyiv to disrupt incoming Russian strikes. The upgrades are aimed at protecting satellite-navigation signals from interference, allowing drones to maintain their programmed flight paths even in areas covered by Ukrainian jamming systems.According to a report by Defense News, Russia is equipping its drones with upgraded Kometa satellite-navigation modules developed by Russian company VNIIR-Progress. The modules use multiple antenna elements to identify and suppress electronic interference, helping drones maintain navigation despite attempts to disrupt their satellite signals.Russia is already using 16-element antenna arrays at scale and preparing 20-element versions for serial production. Ukrainian forces have also detected Shahed-type drones carrying larger 32-element arrays during attacks on Kyiv, the report said, citing Ukrainian electronic-warfare specialist Serhii Beskrestnov.The upgraded Kometa modules use multiple small receiving elements, known as patch antennas, arranged in an array. These elements help the drone distinguish genuine satellite-navigation signals from interference generated by Ukrainian jamming systems.By identifying the direction from which interference originates, the system can suppress unwanted signals while continuing to receive satellite-navigation data. Increasing the number of antenna elements improves the system's ability to filter interference from multiple directions.The larger antenna arrays could make conventional GPS jamming less effective against Russian drones. Ukraine has relied extensively on electronic warfare to disrupt satellite-navigation signals, forcing incoming drones off course or reducing their accuracy.Ukrainian specialists are examining multi-band jamming to disrupt signals across different satellite-navigation frequencies. Another option is GPS spoofing, which involves transmitting false positioning information to mislead a drone's navigation system and divert it from its intended route.Growing threat from Russia's expanding drone arsenalThe antenna upgrades are part of a wider expansion of Russia's drone warfare capabilities. Moscow has been increasing the scale of its Shahed-type drone attacks while introducing faster jet-powered variants, including the Geran-3, Geran-4 and Geran-5.Unlike conventional propeller-driven drones, these variants use turbojet propulsion, allowing some models to reach speeds of up to 600 kmph. Their higher speed reduces the time available for Ukrainian air-defence units to detect, track and intercept incoming threats.The growing use of jet-powered drones is adding pressure on Ukraine's air-defence network, which relies on electronic warfare, mobile air-defence teams and relatively inexpensive interceptor drones to counter Russian aerial attacks.

articles.title: U.K. celebrity accused of sexual misconduct loses legal battle to keep identity secret despite risk of suicide. What happens next?
articles.summary: Lawyers for the male celebrity said he would be "highly likely" to try and kill himself if the allegations were made public.
articles.body:
A male celebrity in the U.K. accused of sexual misconduct against young women has lost a legal battle to prevent the publication of "serious" allegations about him, including potential criminal behavior.

However, in a ruling on Tuesday at London's High Court, a judge ruled that a temporary order preventing his identification should be kept in place to allow for any potential appeal.

The celebrity, who denies the allegations, had taken legal action against two British media companies, Independent Television News (ITN) and the Guardian, to prevent them from publishing the claims and revealing his identity.

His lawyer, Sara Mansoori KC, argued that naming him would be "highly likely" to lead him to try to kill himself, adding that he had previously attempted suicide twice. She said he had "no intention of returning to public life."

Gavin Millar KC, representing the media outlets, argued that the case risks "dragging judges into assessing the causes of suicidal ideation, which are for professionals and not for a judge." He added, "The obligation falls on the hospital to keep him safe, and that's that."

According to Mr Justice Nicklin's judgment , the claims relate to "serious allegations" that took place over a period of years and included "potential criminal activity."

The allegations include "alleged abuse of power, sexual misconduct and inappropriate conduct towards younger or vulnerable persons" as well as the "alleged use of status, influence and access in dealings with women and girls."

Justice Nicklin dismissed his claim on Tuesday, adding, "The court did not determine whether the allegations, or any of them, were true, and the dismissal of the claim does not amount to approval of any publication the defendants may decide to make," the Press Gazette reported.

The judgment added: "It is not substantially disputed that the Claimant has a serious psychiatric vulnerability or that a decision permitting publication, and publication itself, would materially increase his risk of suicide."

But Justice Nicklin said the claimant did not "establish that suicide is inevitable".

Concluding, Justice Nicklin ruled, "The injunction sought would constitute an exceptionally serious interference" of freedom of expression, adding it would "prohibit the Defendants from publishing the results of their investigations into allegations of serious wrongdoing by a prominent individual."

The U.K. has no direct equivalent of the First Amendment. Instead, British courts must balance two competing rights under the European Convention on Human Rights: Article 8, which protects the right to respect for private and family life, and Article 10, which protects freedom of expression.

Neither right automatically takes precedence over the other, meaning judges can weigh a person's privacy interests against the public interest in reporting information about them.

The claimant also cited Article 2, which protects the right to life, and Article 3, which protects against someone being subjected to degrading treatment or punishment. The celebrity said publication of the claims would "expose him to a real and immediate risk of serious harm or death."

Paul Wragg, a Professor of Media Law at the University of Leeds, said, "The application here is unusual because it involves claims of not only privacy under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, but also Article 2, which is the right to life. And therefore, that makes the balancing process slightly more complicated."

He said, "The anonymity claim hinges on the seriousness of the evidence that this is going to have a profound impact upon him, and also speaks to the problem that once this information is out there, it's very difficult to put the genie back in the bottle."

In his judgment, Justice Nicklin said that the "existing anonymity and reporting restrictions order" must remain in force during the period allowed for seeking permission to appeal.

Prof. Wragg said it was "impossible to guess" how long an appeal would take, adding, "It just depends on the court's workload. But if it does go to trial, I don't see us getting a result before next year."

Dan Tench, a litigator at the law firm CMS, said he expected the appeal process to be "quick," adding, "15 or 20 years ago, when privacy law was being actively developed, there were often media cases with pre-publication injunctions which would proceed swiftly up the judicial ladder. In those days, you'd usually expect the Court of Appeal to get on within a week or two. I would expect that to be the case here, possibly even next week. But you cannot be certain."

articles.title: Free film screening to explore climate change to be held in Hull
articles.summary: The National Emergency Briefing, presented by Chris Packham, will be shown at Hull's Guildhall.
articles.body:
A free screening of a film which outlines the impact of climate change both now and in the future will be hosted by Hull City Council.

The National Emergency Briefing, presented by naturalist Chris Packham, will be played at Hull's Guildhall on 24 November followed by a discussion led by council leader Mike Ross and cabinet member for the environment Charles Quinn.

The council said the event would help people to learn more from experts and understand how the council was "responding to the climate and nature emergency".

Quinn said: "Hull is susceptible to the impacts of climate change more than most so it is important the council and the city realises the urgency with which we need to act."

He said: "No prior knowledge on what is happening in Hull is needed and the council looks forward to welcoming residents to learn more and share ideas about what we can all do."

The council said the 50-minute film would also help people learn how they "can stay resilient, as well as actions they can take as individuals and households to combat the crisis."

Those attending would get the chance to support the film by signing an open letter for it to be lobbied to government.

The session will be held from 18:30 GMT on Tuesday 24 November in Room C1 in Hull's Guildhall on Alfred Gelder Street. Doors will open at 18:15.

The council said the event was open to all residents in Hull aged 16 and over, and urged people to register in advance.

articles.title: A US company argued that lawyers using artificial intelligence should receive lower fees after its trade-secrets lawsuit was dismissed; a federal appeals court has upheld a $114,663 award, saying no overbilling was shown
articles.summary: A federal appeals court has ruled that a law firm's use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools does not automatically mean its legal fees should be reduced.
articles.body: A federal appeals court has ruled that a law firm's use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools does not automatically mean its legal fees should be reduced. The court rejected an argument from a losing party that the technology had led to inflated legal bills. The decision by the 10th US Circuit Court of Appeals upholds a legal fee award of $114,663.11 given to defence lawyers in a trade-secrets dispute. The court said anyone challenging a legal bill must provide clear evidence of overcharging. Simply pointing out that a law firm used automated legal software is not enough. Writing for a unanimous three-judge panel, Circuit Judge Carolyn McHugh said AI can make legal research and document writing faster. However, the responsibility to prove that using the technology resulted in unreasonable charges lies with the party challenging the bill. The ruling sets an early example of how courts may deal with the use of automated tools in the legal profession. It makes clear that courts will not automatically assume that using software means lawyers have charged for too many hours.Dismissal leads to fee battleThe dispute over legal fees began with a trade-secrets lawsuit filed by Flux Drive Inc. The company sued defendants from another state, accusing them of taking its privately owned technology without permission. The case never went to trial on the main claims. A federal district court judge in Colorado dismissed the lawsuit after finding that the court did not have legal authority over the Illinois-based defendants. After the case was dismissed, the defendants asked to recover the money they had spent defending themselves. They were represented by the law firm Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck, which submitted detailed records of its legal work and charges to the district court. The trial judge reviewed the records and found that the hours worked and hourly rates were reasonable under federal rules. The judge then ordered Flux Drive to pay $114,663.11 in legal fees. Flux Drive appealed the decision to the 10th Circuit. The company argued that the law firm had used artificial intelligence software while handling the case. It claimed that because AI tools can complete tasks faster, the number of hours charged by the lawyers was too high and placed an unreasonable financial burden on the company.Burden of proof on challengerThe 10th Circuit rejected Flux Drive's argument and upheld the district court's original legal fee award in full. The panel included Circuit Judges Scott Matheson and Richard Federico, along with Judge McHugh. The judges stressed that trial courts have wide powers to decide whether legal fees are reasonable because they directly oversee the cases. "The district court reviewed the time entries and found them reasonable," the panel stated in its opinion. It also noted that Flux Drive had failed to point to specific billing entries that were repeated, false or inflated because of the use of technology. Reuters reported on 2 November that the ruling sets a clear standard for future disputes over legal fees involving technology. Although judges recognise that AI can speed up legal work, anyone seeking to reduce a legal fee award must provide direct evidence showing that the hours charged were unreasonable. Legal analysts say the ruling does not give law firms complete freedom to charge clients for AI-assisted work without question. If someone challenging a bill can show that software completed most of a task in a few minutes while the law firm charged for several hours of manual work, courts still have the power to reduce the fees. However, under the 10th Circuit's standard, simply showing that a law firm used AI software is not enough to overturn a trial court's decision on legal fees.Growing scrutiny of legal technologyThe decision comes at a time when courts are paying closer attention to how law firms use artificial intelligence in their daily work. Over the past two years, federal and state courts across the United States have introduced stricter reporting requirements. These steps followed several cases in which lawyers submitted court documents containing fake legal references generated by AI chatbots that had not been properly checked. The 10th Circuit has also recently proposed changes to its rules. Under these proposed changes, lawyers would have to formally confirm that a human attorney had independently checked all legal authorities cited in their appeals court filings. These administrative rules are aimed at maintaining accuracy and preventing lawyers from misleading courts. However, the Flux Drive case deals with a different issue. It focuses on how law firms charge clients when they use technology to complete legal work. By upholding the $114,663 award, the court confirmed that existing methods for deciding reasonable legal fees remain valid, whether a law firm uses traditional research methods or modern software. The 10th Circuit's formal order leaves the district court's fee decision unchanged, bringing the legal dispute between Flux Drive and the defence lawyers to an end.You use AI every day. articles.title: How 'mogging' went from toxic term to mainstream
articles.summary: Mogging, named Collins English Dictionary's word of the year, was once the preserve of the manosphere but has become part of everyday discourse.
articles.body:
"Mogging" has seen its usage soar over the past year, with the Gen Z slang term being named Collins English Dictionary's word of the year.

Finding its origins in the online language of the manosphere, an online community built around hyper-masculine and often misogynistic content, the term broke out into the mainstream this year, being used by celebrities and the media.

The word is defined by Collins as being used playfully to mean "the act of outshining or outperforming someone or something" and is now widely employed in online discourse about celebrity culture, with signs it is making its way into everyday vocabulary.

"I heard someone the other day say they were 'walk-mogged' - basically just someone else in the street about their age walking faster than them," says Tony Thorne, a language consultant at King's College London.

The term has grown in usage through its association with Clavicular, an influencer known for "looksmaxxing" content, who recently pleaded not guilty to charges including rape . He regularly posts clips of himself attempting to "mog" people in public spaces.

The word reached a wider audience when posts describing the controversial streamer as having been "brutally frame mogged" went viral earlier this year.

But "mogging" may be a lot older than its recent surge might suggest.

Thorne explains that the term - often traced back to the acronym AMOG, or Alpha Male of the Group - was originally used in the 2010s on bodybuilding and incel (involuntary celibate) message boards, before being co-opted by a younger, broader audience.

"It was a toxic term about extreme competitiveness, the urge to dominate. People then started to use it ironically and teasingly."

In a nod to its origins, Hollywood royalty and seven-time Mr Olympia, Arnold Schwarzenegger, posted footage of himself in his bodybuilding heyday earlier this year, along with the ironic caption "someone just tried to explain this new trend 'frame mogging' to me..." .

Slang terms breaking out of the community that coins them isn't unprecedented.

"It's becoming more like the drag queen slang that was also used until recently - 'it was lit', 'she slays', 'he's a king', 'she's a queen'. It's become part of that more sort of silly, kind celebrity-type banter," says Thorne.

He believes that the term has now "largely been detoxified" as it mostly "retains that tinge of mockery or irony".

"I can't speak for all the instances when it's used, but for young people I know who are using it today, there is not anything unhealthy about it anymore."

Reflecting this softer and more mainstream meaning, British Vogue captioned their photo of Heated Rivalry actor Hudson Williams arriving at the 2026 Golden Globes as him "mogging at the Golden Globes".

And in an interview earlier this year, figure skater Alysa Liu said her "main goal for this competition was to mog".

At its heart, there still remains a competitive element to how the word is used to frame a situation.

"The language still retains this element of hyper-individual, competitive performance culture. It's still got that element," says Thorne.

A recent online debate was sparked between fans comparing People magazine's choice for 2026's sexiest man alive, The Pitt actor Noah Wyle, with the 2025 winner, Wicked star Jonathan Bailey.

Last year, fans of Zara Larsson and Tate McRae pitched the two singers against each other after the Swedish popstar opened for McRae on the North American leg of latter's Miss Possessive tour.

Some fans viewed Larsson's performance as having "mogged" McRae, despite being a support act.

Larsson later pushed back on the comparison, speaking about her respect for McRae during an interview on the Call Her Daddy podcast.

Another famous face that has been brought into the mogging debate is Cillian Murphy, with the Irish actor being compared favourably to his co-stars by some.

However, there are signs the term is starting to break beyond pitting people against one another to be used to simply mean someone is appearing commanding.

During her appearance on Celebrity Traitors, some online commentary referred to Maya Jama mogging - even while hanging out of a helicopter.

"When it's used in this gushing celebrity context, it's a bit like using 'slay' - 'she's a queen, she slays'," says Thorne.

Mogging can also take many forms and refer to someone excelling in any number of different ways.

"I think there are all sorts of opportunities - style-mogging, height-mogging, car-mogging," says Thorne. "You can apply [mogging] to almost anything now."

'Mogging' is Collins' word of the year... but do you know what it means?

articles.title: 1.5-tonne Nasa space observatory set to crash on Earth today, possibility of debris parts falling in India
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A 1.5-tonne space observatory of Nasa is heading back to Earth on Wednesday after working in space for 22 years and some parts of its debris
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A 1.5-tonne space observatory of Nasa is heading back to Earth on Wednesday after working in space for 22 years and some parts of its debris could fall in southern India.Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory was launched in 2004 to explore the universe’s most powerful explosions called gamma-ray bursts. When launched, the spacecraft was a first-of-its-kind multiwavelength observatory designed to study the most powerful explosions in the cosmos using its three telescopes.“US Space Force predicted that the spacecraft will re-enter the atmosphere at approximately 3:30 a.m. EST, Nov. 4, with an uncertainty of 11 hours,” Nasa said on Monday.The US space agency expects most of the spacecraft to burn up as it travels through the atmosphere, but some components are expected to survive re-entry.Most surviving debris is expected to fall into the ocean. However, parts of India, Africa, Australia, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America could fall within the possible re-entry zone. The re-entry band spans between 20.6°N and 20.6°S latitude, which covers parts of southern India (including cities like Mumbai, Hyderabad, Bengaluru, Chennai, Bhubaneswar and Kochi).Isro has not said anything if it is tracking the descending space telescope. “If 70% of the Earth is ocean, 30% is land. So three out of 10 times it's on land, not ocean,” Brad Tucker, an astrophysicist at Australian National University, told ABC News.The Nasa observatory was originally designed for a two-year prime mission. However, the spacecraft was able to conduct science operations for more than two decades. Swift served as a multi-tool for exploring the universe, observing a wide range of light, rapidly pointing at short-lived outbursts, and sending alerts to other facilities to help coordinate follow-up observations.“The observatory has broadened our understanding of a wide variety of cosmic objects and events, from active galaxies powered by supermassive black holes and stars undergoing X-ray flares, to supernova explosions and comets and asteroids in our own solar system,” Nasa said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Who is Jason Turkish? Haley Stevens’ fiancé makes late-night phone calls after Dem Congresswoman endorses Republican Mike Rogers abandoning El-Sayed
articles.summary: The fiancé of Democratic Congresswoman Haley Stevens has pushed back allegations that he influenced her decision to abandon fellow Democrat Abdul El-Sayed
articles.body: The fiancé of Democratic Congresswoman Haley Stevens has pushed back allegations that he influenced her decision to abandon fellow Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and endorse Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers in Michigan, triggering a political storm just days before the November 3 midterm elections.Jason Turkish, a disability rights lawyer and Democratic donor, made a series of late-night phone calls on Monday to counter claims by Stevens’ former staffers, friends and political allies that he had played an outsized role in her political decisions. The controversy intensified after Stevens, who had initially promised to support El-Sayed following her defeat in the Democratic Senate primary, unexpectedly appeared alongside Rogers at a Detroit church service on Sunday and announced her endorsement of the Republican.Turkish had endorsed Rogers several days earlier, citing concerns about El-Sayed’s criticism of Israel and its military campaign in Gaza. His endorsement had already raised questions about a possible rift within the couple, but Stevens’ decision to back the same Republican prompted accusations that Turkish had pressured her into changing her position.Turkish has rejected the allegations, while Stevens has insisted that her endorsement was entirely her own decision.Who is Jason Turkish and what are the allegations against him?Turkish, 39, is a disability rights lawyer and political fundraiser who works as managing partner at Nyman Turkish, a litigation and disability law firm based in Southfield, Michigan. He lives in Huntington Woods, a suburb north of Detroit. According to The Washington Post, he and Stevens met through a mutual friend, David Kramer, after her 2022 re-election campaign.Their relationship reportedly became closer during Stevens’ Senate campaign, which began in 2025. The couple were said to have become engaged secretly around June, although their engagement was not publicly announced until after Stevens lost the Democratic primary.Turkish was initially known to Stevens’ campaign team as a major donor. However, several former campaign staffers told The Washington Post that he gradually became one of her closest advisers and began involving himself in campaign decisions.According to multiple people familiar with the campaign, senior staffers became concerned about his growing influence around June. They reportedly held a meeting without Stevens to discuss ways to limit his involvement with the campaign.Former staffers alleged that Turkish criticized campaign employees over their work, including digital fundraising and campaign messaging. He reportedly summoned a senior digital campaign employee to his law office and shouted at her over the content being produced and the fundraising emails being sent.Stevens, 43, lost the Democratic Senate nomination to Abdul El-Sayed, 42, in August. The primary exposed significant differences between the two candidates, particularly over their positions on Israel and the war in Gaza. Stevens represented the more centrist wing of the Democratic Party, while El-Sayed ran on a progressive platform. His criticism of Israel's military campaign in Gaza, which he has described as genocide, became a major point of disagreement.Rep Jamie Raskin, a Maryland Democrat, said he spoke to Stevens for 25 minutes on Saturday night. According to him, she indicated that she was committed to the Democratic Party and would celebrate with them on election night.But within hours, the situation changed dramatically. Stevens appeared alongside Rogers at a church service in Detroit and announced her endorsement of the Republican Senate candidate.The Republican candidate's campaign was reportedly caught off guard as well. A Rogers spokesperson said the campaign learnt about the endorsement when Stevens' video appeared online.President Donald Trump praised Stevens as brave and said he would like to see her join the Republican Party. House Speaker Mike Johnson also reportedly sent her a message after the announcement.'Her fiancé had taken her phone away'One of the most serious allegations came from Jordan Acker, a University of Michigan regent and a friend of Stevens.Acker said he had spoken to Stevens several times on Saturday, including on the morning of the endorsement. According to him, she had indicated that she intended to remain silent about the Senate race. He questioned what had changed in the following two hours.Acker also raised concerns about Turkish's treatment of Stevens' friends, staff members and political allies. When someone on X suggested that he should speak to Stevens privately, Acker responded that her fiancé had taken her phone away.Turkish strongly disputed the allegation in his conversation with The Daily Beast.He instead questioned Acker's conduct, bringing up a controversy involving the University of Michigan regent several months earlier. The university had investigated Acker following reports that he made sexual comments about a Democratic strategist and vulgar remarks about a female student.Turkish said Acker had been calling and texting Stevens repeatedly. He claimed she had tolerated the contact out of compassion because Acker was struggling following the controversy."She has tried to provide him the support that he needs as he, you know, seeks to move on from that episode," Turkish said.Stevens rejects claims that her fiancé made the decision for herStevens has also directly addressed suggestions that Turkish influenced her political decision.In an 890-word statement posted on X late Monday, she defended her endorsement of Rogers and accused critics of undermining her independence by attributing her decision to her relationship.She argued that she had reached her own conclusion that El-Sayed was not fit to serve in the US Senate."Think about what that says. A woman can serve in Congress, run statewide, and fight for her convictions, and still be told that when she makes a choice people dislike, someone else must be pulling the strings," she wrote.She described such suggestions as "sexism dressed up as political analysis". Stevens also maintained that she had been increasingly marginalized by El-Sayed's campaign and that her decision reflected her disagreement with his positions and his handling of the Israel issue.You use AI every day. articles.title: Rotten-egg smell has plagued Florida residents for years; now, county moves to sue landfill operator and state agency after study points to Mount Dora site as likely source
articles.summary: Residents living near a landfill in Florida have been complaining about a persistent rotten-egg-like smell for years, claiming it has disrupted their
articles.body: Residents living near a landfill in Florida have been complaining about a persistent rotten-egg-like smell for years, claiming it has disrupted their daily lives and raised concerns about the quality of the air they breathe and the water they drink. Now, Lake County commissioners are taking legal action against the landfill operator and the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) over the issue.According to a report by WKMG News 6, commissioners unanimously voted to move forward with a lawsuit involving Mid Florida Landfill near Mount Dora. The facility, located off Robie Avenue near the Sullivan Ranch community, is operated by Hubbard Construction.The decision comes after years of complaints from nearby residents, who say the strong odour has become increasingly difficult to tolerate. Some have described it as resembling sulfur or rotten eggs, claiming that it can be detected even inside their homes.Residents say unbearable landfill odour is affecting daily lifeResidents of Sullivan Ranch say the smell has become a persistent problem, affecting their everyday routines and making it difficult to enjoy their homes.One resident told News 6 that the odour had been an ongoing issue for a long time, adding that it was noticeable even inside the house after waking up.Caleb Swallow, who lives in the Sullivan Ranch neighbourhood near the landfill, has also spoken publicly about the problem. Pointing to the facility, he told the news outlet, "It's literally right behind the dump. You can smell it right now, just standing back here."Swallow believes state environmental regulators should take stronger action to address the situation. He said he had previously suggested that the county consider legal action against the Florida Department of Environmental Protection to ensure it fulfils its regulatory responsibilities.2025 study identifies landfill as source of the smellThe complaints eventually prompted the City of Mount Dora to investigate the source of the persistent odour. A 2025 study identified the Mid Florida Landfill as the likely source of the widespread smell affecting nearby communities.Despite the findings, residents say the problem has continued, with the situation becoming more noticeable as the landfill has expanded and new residential developments have come up in the surrounding area.Mandy Richardson, another Sullivan Ranch resident, told News 6 that the complaints had increased because of the landfill's growing size and the expansion of nearby communities."The complaints are getting much worse because the dump has just grown and grown in size, and there's more development, so there's more communities being affected than just ours," she said.Residents raise concerns about air quality and drinking waterApart from the unpleasant smell, residents and county commissioners have expressed concerns about the landfill's potential environmental impact, particularly on air quality and drinking water.Richardson said the possibility of contamination was frightening for families living in the area and called on local authorities to introduce stronger regulations."The fear for the future of what that could hold for our drinking water and the air that we breathe is really frightening," she told the news outlet. She added that it was critical for the county and city to step in and address the concerns.The proposed lawsuit is intended to push for action against the landfill operator as well as the state environmental regulator. County leaders have said their efforts to work with the operator have not brought the issue to a satisfactory resolution.What have the landfill operator and Florida authorities said?The Florida Department of Environmental Protection told News 6 that it does not comment on pending litigation.The landfill operator, Hubbard Construction, had not responded to News 6's request for comment on the proposed lawsuit at the time of its report.However, the company had previously defended its operations. In an earlier statement reported by WESH in 2025, Hubbard Construction said its facility remained in compliance with applicable environmental regulations and that it worked closely with state regulators and inspectors. The company also disputed allegations concerning odour and erosion control.With commissioners now agreeing unanimously to pursue legal action, residents hope the move will finally bring relief to neighbourhoods that have dealt with the persistent smell for years.You use AI every day. articles.title: A 14-year-old boy confessed to a double murder after two days of police questioning in 1977; he was pardoned in 2014 after decades in prison, but a 2026 appeals court granted immunity to the officers he sued
articles.summary: A murder investigation in Peoria, Illinois, in 1977 changed the course of a 14-year-old boy’s life.
articles.body: A murder investigation in Peoria, Illinois, in 1977 changed the course of a 14-year-old boy’s life. Johnnie Lee Savory was taken in for questioning after two teenagers were found murdered, and after more than a day of interrogation, he confessed to the killings. His first conviction was later overturned because the confession was found to be involuntary, but a second trial resulted in another conviction. He spent decades behind bars before being released on parole in 2006 and pardoned in 2014. Nearly half a century after the killings, a civil rights case brought by Savory reached the Seventh Circuit, which ruled in August 2026 that the former officers were entitled to immunity.A 29-hour police interrogation ended with a 14-year-old confessing to two murdersAs reported by Illinois Courts, the case began on 18 January 1977, when 19-year-old Connie Cooper and her 14-year-old brother, James Robinson, were found stabbed to death at their home in Peoria. Their mother and stepfather discovered the bodies at around 4 pm. Police collected several items from the property, including a black nightstick, a pipe, blood samples and hairs found in different parts of the house.About a week later, investigators Edgar Haynes and George Pinkney learnt that Savory had spent time with Robinson on the evening before the murders. News footage also showed him at the property after the killings. The officers subsequently visited his school and asked him to accompany them to the police station. Although he was initially reluctant to answer questions, he agreed to go.What followed lasted approximately 29 hours from the time officers first met him at school until he confessed. Detectives questioned him in shifts, showed him photographs from the crime scene and challenged his answers. He also spoke briefly with his probation officer that evening. Police then arranged a polygraph examination, telling him he could go home after completing it.The US Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit reported, the first examination took place late that night. Savory was given his Miranda warnings at around 11.30 pm and said he did not want to continue speaking to police. The questioning stopped, but he was held overnight at a detention centre. His father was informed around midnight. Savory slept for several hours before being taken back to the police department the following morning.The questioning resumed after officers read him his rights again. He met with his father and was later asked to undergo another polygraph test. During that examination, private examiner Ed Bowers reportedly raised his voice, moved close to the teenager and accused him of being a murderer. Savory subsequently stood by a window and cried. At 7.35 pm, he confessed to the two killings. He later changed his account and denied involvement.His first conviction was overturned, but a second trial brought another guilty verdictSavory was charged with two counts of first-degree murder in February 1977. His first trial ended with a conviction, but the Illinois appellate court overturned it in 1980, finding that his confession had not been voluntary.Savory was tried again in 1981, with the second case including testimony from members of the Ivy family. Three witnesses, Tina, Ella and Frank Ivy, told the jury that Savory had said he accidentally cut Robinson but left him alive. As reported, the jury found him guilty again, and he received a prison sentence of 40 to 80 years.Questions about the witness accounts emerged in the years that followed. Tina and Frank Ivy signed affidavits in 1983 withdrawing their earlier testimony. Frank later provided another affidavit in 2003, saying his testimony at the second trial had been incorrect and that an officer had pressured him to make false statements.Savory also pursued legal efforts to obtain access to physical evidence from the murders. He sought DNA testing of hairs collected at the scene and a piece cut from a pair of blue trousers taken from his father. A court granted his request in 2012, but the original material was no longer available for testing because it had not been preserved by the police department. Testing of the remaining trousers did not show blood.He was released on parole in 2006 after spending around three decades in prison. In 2014, while a motion seeking a new trial was pending, Illinois Governor Patrick Quinn granted him a pardon. The pardon came after years of efforts to challenge the conviction, although it did not amount to a judicial finding that the second conviction was wrongful.Savory's civil rights lawsuit targeted police conductIn 2017, Savory brought a federal civil rights action against 16 former Peoria police officers, the City of Peoria and Bowers. He relied on Section 1983 of federal law, which allows individuals to seek redress when someone acting under state authority violates their constitutional rights.His allegations covered several aspects of the investigation. He claimed that police had unlawfully detained him, obtained his confession through coercive questioning and mishandled evidence that might have helped establish his innocence. He also alleged that officers had fabricated evidence, including reports of statements attributed to him and accounts from witnesses.The case initially faced a major procedural obstacle when it was dismissed as being outside the applicable limitation period. That decision was reversed by the Seventh Circuit sitting en banc in 2020, allowing the lawsuit to proceed. It was subsequently transferred to the US District Court for the Central District of Illinois.The defendants sought summary judgment, arguing that they were protected by qualified or absolute immunity. The district court rejected their request. It found that factual disagreements prevented it from resolving the unlawful detention claim at that stage and that existing legal standards could have alerted the officers and Bowers to the constitutional problems with their conduct. It also considered the allegations concerning missing and allegedly fabricated evidence sufficient to prevent the defendants from obtaining judgment in their favour.The officers and Bowers appealed that decision. The case, Savory v Andrews, was heard by the US Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit, with arguments taking place on 11 September 2025. The court issued its ruling on 14 August 2026.Seventh Circuit finds the officers were entitled to qualified immunityThe appeals court reversed the district court's decision, concluding that the officers could not be held liable on the claims under consideration. Its reasoning centred on qualified immunity, a legal protection that can shield public officials from civil liability when their conduct did not violate a constitutional right that was clearly established at the time.On the unlawful detention claim, the majority concluded that the officers had at least arguable probable cause. It considered the information available to investigators, including Savory's association with Robinson, his presence at the crime scene after the killings, the hairs collected from the property and statements reportedly made to police by a reporter and Savory's foster mother.The court said officers could reasonably rely on those accounts when assessing whether there was a basis to detain him. It also pointed out that Savory had not produced evidence showing that the officers had fabricated the reporter's or foster mother's statements. On that basis, the majority held that the officers were entitled to qualified immunity.The judges also addressed the missing physical evidence. Savory had argued that police officers were responsible for the disappearance of the fabric sample from the trousers and hairs collected from the victims' hands. The majority found that the available record did not establish when those items had been destroyed or whether officers had acted in bad faith.Under the constitutional standards applied by the court, the destruction of potentially useful evidence does not automatically establish a due process violation. The circumstances, including whether the material had apparent exculpatory value and whether it was deliberately destroyed in bad faith, matter. The court found that Savory had not supplied enough specific evidence to establish those requirements.Court says earlier rulings did not clearly prohibit the interrogation methodsThe confession claim presented a separate question. The majority acknowledged that Savory had been questioned for many hours over two days, had undergone polygraph examinations and had been subjected to aggressive questioning. However, it examined whether legal decisions already in existence in 1977 had made the alleged conduct clearly unconstitutional.Savory relied on earlier US Supreme Court decisions involving the interrogation of children. One was Haley v Ohio, a 1948 case concerning a 15-year-old questioned by police for five hours overnight. Another was Gallegos v Colorado, decided in 1962, involving a 14-year-old held for five days without access to a lawyer, parent or another supportive adult.The Seventh Circuit majority distinguished those cases from Savory's circumstances. It pointed out that officers had given him Miranda warnings, including information about his right to legal counsel. When he initially said he did not wish to speak, the questioning stopped. He was also able to meet with his father and probation officer before making his confession.The judges therefore concluded that the earlier decisions did not put the alleged unconstitutionality of the interrogation beyond debate. The fact that Savory was a child and had been questioned for an extended period was not enough, in the majority's assessment, to establish that the officers should have known their particular methods violated the Constitution.The same reasoning applied to Bowers. Although he was a private polygraph examiner rather than a police officer, the court considered the allegations against him in the context of the interrogation. It found that the legal position at the time did not clearly establish that his alleged conduct was unconstitutional, even if he had participated in an effort to obtain a confession.Officers also receive absolute immunity over their trial testimonyThe court considered Savory's allegations that officers had fabricated police reports recording statements attributed to him. He argued that the reports and subsequent testimony had contributed to violations of his right to a fair trial.The majority drew a distinction between allegedly false investigative material and evidence actually used against a defendant in court. It found that the reports in question had not been introduced or relied upon at Savory's criminal trial. As a result, their creation did not establish the required connection to a violation of his right to a fair trial.The judges also addressed the officers' testimony. Even if officers had given evidence consistent with allegedly fabricated reports, they could not be held civilly liable on the basis of their trial testimony alone. Witnesses are generally protected by absolute immunity for statements made while testifying in court, including police officers.The ruling therefore extended beyond the qualified immunity arguments concerning the interrogation and detention. The officers also retained absolute immunity against the particular claim based on their testimony at trial.A dissenting judge disagreed with the majority's reasoningThe August 2026 decision was not unanimous in every respect. Circuit Judge Candace Jackson-Akiwumi agreed with the outcome on the destruction of evidence claim and the protection afforded to officers for their trial testimony, but disagreed with the majority on the unlawful detention and coerced confession claims.You use AI every day. articles.title: Lorry driver electrocuted after vehicle hit overhead power line
articles.summary: Andy Lloyd was electrocuted when he got out of the cab and came into contact with the metal step.
articles.body:
A driver of a tipper lorry was electrocuted after part of his vehicle hit an overhead power line, an inquest has heard.

Andy Lloyd, 56, who ran a family business, was delivering a load of hardcore to a farm with his 14-year-old son when the grab arm on his truck came into contact with the 11,000-volt overhead cables.

Ruthin Coroner's Court heard Lloyd, from Bod Elian, Llanelian in Conwy, climbed down from the cab and was electrocuted when he came into contact with the metal step.

He was pronounced dead at the scene in Tan y Dderwen Farm in Betws-yn-Rhos, Conwy on 1 May - less than a month before he was due to get married.

The inquest heard that Lloyd's son, who cannot be named for legal reasons, had joined his dad in the lorry that day to gain work experience.

Senior coroner John Gittins for North Wales East and Central read from the teenager's statement.

He said his dad had moved the lorry closer to where contractors were erecting a shed to tip the load when the grab arm hit the power line.

The court heard the teenager had tried to tell his dad, but Lloyd had already exited the cab.

Contractors who witnessed the incident described seeing flames coming from the rear tyres of the lorry and Lloyd's boots before he collapsed.

One of the men then noticed the teenager in the lorry and helped him exit safely.

Another performed CPR on Lloyd while the third called an ambulance.

The inquest heard that Devon Locke, a Scottish Power engineer, had been dispatched to the area to investigate after the supply had been tripped.

When he saw the emergency vehicles at the farm he learned what had happened and saw the lorry was still in contact with the cables running above the field.

Although the power had been tripped plans were made to make the line safe.

The coroner concluded that Lloyd died as a result of an accident and offered his condolences to his family.

Lloyd's partner, Hayley Lloyd, said in her statement that his "last moments were spent in his truck with his son beside him" and that he "cared quietly but fiercely for those around him."

articles.title: 77% of US voters fear AI election manipulation: Why deepfakes are raising alarm ahead of 2026 midterms
articles.summary: Political campaigns across the United States have entered a new digital era during the 2026 midterm elections.
articles.body: Political campaigns across the United States have entered a new digital era during the 2026 midterm elections. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is no longer just an experimental technology. It is now being used as an active tool in political campaigns.From realistic fake audio recordings targeting candidates just hours before polling begins to automated tools that create and target AI-generated video ads, the technology is making it harder for voters to decide what information they can trust. Election monitors and political strategists are struggling to deal with an online environment where genuine campaign material is becoming increasingly difficult to separate from computer-generated content.Public concern about the impact of AI-generated media has reached high levels. A survey by the Bipartisan Policy Center found that 77 per cent of voters were deeply concerned about the use of artificial intelligence to spread false information or influence public opinion during this election cycle. The findings show that voters across the political spectrum share these concerns, with majorities from both major parties identifying deepfakes and automated persuasion as serious threats to fair elections.These concerns have also started changing campaign strategies. Axios reported last week that Democratic groups had launched a $4 million advertising campaign across four competitive House of Representatives districts. The campaign was designed to test whether voters support stricter rules for artificial intelligence.Deepfakes blur the line between real and fakeOne of the biggest changes in the 2026 midterms is how easily people can now create realistic fake content. In earlier election cycles, changing digital images or recordings required special technical skills and expensive computer systems. Today, widely available software allows campaign workers or outside groups to copy a politician's voice or create convincing videos using simple written instructions.During the autumn campaign season, AI-generated content appeared in several closely contested races. Fake audio recordings designed to sound like candidates making controversial statements were shared through messaging apps. Some were released shortly before important debates, giving fact-checkers little time to check them before they spread further.Fake videos have also become part of negative political campaigns. Instead of using traditional edited footage, some AI-generated advertisements show completely fictional scenes. These videos may depict candidates taking part in unpopular activities or appearing alongside controversial public figures.The spread of such material has created more work for election officials and news organisations. Fact-checkers now have to spend time checking whether audio recordings and videos are genuine before examining the political claims they contain. This has slowed down political reporting and made it harder to respond quickly to misleading content.Machine learning changes how campaigns target votersApart from creating public-facing fake content, political campaigns are also using machine-learning systems to improve how they reach voters. These tools analyse large amounts of information, including shopping habits, social media activity and past voting records. They can then create messages aimed at specific groups of people.Traditional political advertising usually targets broad groups based on factors such as age or location. AI tools can go much further by creating personalised messages for smaller groups and even individual voters. Algorithms can produce thousands of different versions of an advertisement in real time, changing the words, images and emotional tone to match what a particular voter is likely to respond to.This allows campaigns to test different messages and quickly identify which ones work best. Political teams can run hundreds of online advertisements at the same time and stop using ineffective versions within minutes. They can make these decisions by tracking how people respond to the advertisements.However, researchers warn that this type of automated targeting could increase political divisions. When different groups receive completely different political messages, voters may end up seeing very different versions of the same issue. This could create separate information bubbles and make it harder for people to understand opposing views.Voters struggle to identify AI-generated contentThe growing use of AI-generated material in political discussions has left many voters unsure about the information they see and hear. As fake videos become more realistic, signs that once exposed digital editing are becoming harder to spot. These included unusual lighting, strange eye movements and distorted background sounds.Election security experts warn that the growing gap between AI technology and tools designed to detect fake content has created another problem. It is known as the "liar's dividend". This happens when politicians or public figures can deny genuine but embarrassing recordings by falsely claiming that they were created using artificial intelligence.Research by the Bipartisan Policy Center shows that voter concerns go beyond the possibility of being fooled by realistic fake videos. People are also worried about the wider loss of trust in official information. When voters begin to believe that almost any recording could be fake, their confidence in genuine sources, including candidate speeches and official debates, can also fall.Major technology companies have introduced digital watermarks and automated systems to identify and label AI-generated content. However, these tools are not perfect. Altered videos and recordings can still spread on decentralised online platforms before detection systems identify them.You use AI every day. articles.title: Council launches review after flood barriers not used during Storm Boelo
articles.summary: A report to Renfrewshire Council confirmed forecasts before Storm Boelo 'significantly underestimated tidal levels on the R110iver Clyde'.
articles.body:
Renfrewshire Council will carry out a full review of its flood prevention arrangements after flood barriers were not used during Storm Boelo.

A report to the local authority confirmed forecasts before the storm "significantly underestimated tidal levels on the River Clyde".

As a result, no flood warning was issued and part of a multi-million pound defence scheme was not activated.

Local business owners later hit out at the local authority and told BBC Scotland News their premises had suffered serious damage.

The southern plant room, which controls the Renfrew Bridge, also suffered extensive damage, rendering the swing bridge inoperable .

It is expected to be closed to road users for months.

The council said it would now undertake "a comprehensive review" in partnership with the Scottish Environment Protection Agency (Sepa) and other stakeholders.

It added this would help to "understand why the actual level of the River Clyde differed so significantly from forecast levels".

The review will also seek to "identify any improvements required to forecasting arrangements, warning systems, operational protocols and wider flood resilience measures".

The council said 13 businesses in the area suffered water ingress impact, although 10 are now back operating.

It said it had offered support to every business it had been able to contact.

The local authority also confirmed eight of the businesses affected were based on the river side of the barriers on Ferry Road.

No flood warnings were issued by Sepa for Renfrew ahead of Storm Boelo, which affected Scotland from 24 to 26 October .

And no concerns regarding exceptional tidal levels were raised through other partners.

However, the evening tide was recorded at 4.49m (14.72ft) - the highest since digital records began there in 1998.

That was about double the projected forecast of 2.2m to 2.42m (7.2ft to 7.9ft), figures below the council's 3.9m (12.8ft) threshold for raising the barriers.

The forecast also fell below the council threshold for sending staff to the barrier to assess the situation in person.

The council report said the decision not to use the barriers had followed "an established process" developed through "operational experience, historic events and flood risk assessments".

In the aftermath of the extreme weather the Renfrew Bridge was forced to close, but the council said this was unrelated to the flood barrier.

The bridge opened in May 2025 and is within its two-year defects period.

Both the contractor and the council's insurers are now investigating whether a defect was responsible for water getting in.

The review will also assess whether raising the barriers more often as a precaution could disrupt the local community.

The threshold for sending council staff to look at the barriers during bad weather has currently been reduced as a temporary measure while the review is carried out.

Gordon McNeil, the council's director of environment, housing and infrastructure, said: "While the report shows in some detail that officers followed the established procedures correctly... it is important we work with our partners to understand why the forecasting was significantly different from what we subsequently experienced."

He added the local authority would consider if a "more prudent approach" was needed in the future.

The £10m North Renfrew Flood Prevention Scheme was introduced in 2016 to reduce flood risk to homes, businesses and infrastructure in the area.

The scheme comprises a pumping station at Mill Burn on Fingal Road - which was in use during the storm - a 1km-long, 2.3m (7.5ft) high embankment and two barriers, built into Ferry Road and Fishers Road.

articles.title: After 25 years as a domestic worker, Martha Matilda Harper saved $360 to open a Rochester, NY salon in 1888; she pioneered modern franchising
articles.summary: Discover the inspiring story of Martha Matilda Harper, a domestic worker who became a salon owner and franchising pioneer, transforming women's hair care and empowering women in the 19th century.
articles.body: In the late nineteenth century, women usually cared for their hair at home, with some brushing, homemade remedies, oils and beeswax. The idea of going into a shop for a scalp treatment was often ignored or far beyond their reach. Then a woman named Martha Matilda Harper changed that. Harper spent about 25 years in domestic service before she opened her first salon in Rochester, New York, in 1888. She used $360 of her own savings, roughly $10,000 in today’s money, according to UNH Paul College. Harper relied on a hair tonic formula passed down by a doctor she had once worked for. Researchers at the Kellogg School of Management at Northwestern University describe her as the founder of the franchise model for business growth and say that she built this business model to help and lift young women out of poverty and domestic service by turning them into business owners.From domestic worker to a salon owner Martha Matilda Harper was born in 1857 in Ontario, Canada. She was sent out to work as a domestic worker at the age of seven. She worked in domestic service for nearly a quarter of a century, first in Ontario and then in Rochester, where she arrived in 1882. Along the way, she also worked for a doctor who taught her how a clean, well-stimulated scalp supports healthy hair. Later on, inspired by the doctor’s method, she came up with the herbal tonic recipe that she later built a business around.First hair salon in the city Rochester was also a home to Susan B. Anthony and a lively circle of women activists. Harper was encouraged to strike out on her own. In 1888, she set up shop in the Powers Building in downtown Rochester, a prestigious address picked to draw the city’s social elite and opened the first public hair care salon in the area. Her own floor-length hair worked as her advertisement. In the shop, she hired women from the same background she came from, including former servants who were trained in her methods. Women who visited from other cities wanted a Harper shop in their own communities and that created an issue familiar to any successful shop owner.The franchise ideaRather than open branches and run them all herself, Harper offered ownership to women she trained. According to the Rochester Museum & Science Centre’s guide to her papers, the first franchise shop opened in Buffalo, New York, in 1891 and more than 500 Harper Method shops opened in the United States and overseas during her lifetime. The owners were known as Harperites. They learned a method built around cleanliness, scalp stimulation and exercise and used only Harper products.Training did not stop after opening day. The company held reunions, continuing education sessions and the monthly magazine kept owners informed about business matters while building the sense of community among them. It is fair to call her a franchise pioneer; the model did not become a dominant way of extending a business until decades after her salons first opened.A lasting legacy The National Women’s Hall of Fame says hundreds of women became shop owners by buying into her network through flexible financing and thousands more trained and worked in it. Her system combined centralised management, quality control and independent ownership. The hall also credits her with employment practices that were unusual for the period, including child care, evening hours, flexible time, profit sharing and paid personal time off.Harper mainly relied on naturally occurring substances and refused the newer chemical hair dyes and synthetic permanents. The Rochester Museum & Science Center credits her with the invention of the reclining shampoo chair and the basin with a neck cutout, though she never patented either, so she never received legal recognition for them.Just like that, in her own community, she became the first woman member of the Rochester Chamber of Commerce and her customers reportedly included Susan B. Anthony and President Calvin Coolidge, who is said to have visited her Paris shop for scalp massages. Harper died in 1950 and the business she started carried on until 1972. A woman who had spent roughly 25 years as a house worker opened a salon in Rochester, which gained quite a success in its time and also helped many women financially.You use AI every day. articles.title: Right to protest can't justify endless occupation of a site: SC
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court on Tuesday said no group, political party, NGO or civil society outfit could occupy a protest site indefinitely.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court on Tuesday said no group, political party, NGO or civil society outfit could occupy a protest site indefinitely.A bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said there were competing fundamental rights right to carry on trade and business and right to free speech and expression when senior advocate Mukul Rohatgi, appearing for traders, said the court must restrain all parties, NGO and civil society groups from holding protests in Delhi for the next two months to enable businesses to resume and to ensure that workers got their due.The court asked a traders’ association, which has sought Rs 1,000 crore in damages due to protests by CJP and opposition INDIA bloc during the festive season, to implead the protest organisers in the case for determination of compensation and how it is apportioned if it is awarded.Solicitor general Tushar Mehta said those who call for bandhs and agitations must bear responsibility towards compensating the loss caused to others. The bench asked Rohatgi to make the individuals, organisations and political parties responsible for protests and the resultant closure of shops parties in the petition.When senior advocates Menaka Guruswamy, Arundhati Katju, N Hariharan and others simultaneously argued that protests were part of the right to free speech and right of dissent in a democracy, the bench said, “The right to protest and right to trade and business are both constitutionally recognised fundamental rights. We are not talking about trade in the commercial sense.”CJI Kant said, “We are talking in terms of the source of livelihood of daily wagers, hawkers, rediwalas, sabziwalas – where will they go? Hence, a protest site must be identified which allows people to protest without hampering the livelihood of daily wagers.” The CJI emphasised that the right to protest was not an absolute right. “One set of protesters cannot occupy a designated protest site for all times to come... Everyone has a right to protest and they should be given a definite time period to protest...,” he added.Mehta said, “Calling for a protest without permission and asking people to march to Parliament cannot be permitted.” On denotification of Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site, Delhi Police commissioner Anurag Kumar said the decision was taken based on the recommendations of a committee constituted following the SC’s July 2018 order for regulating protests at Jantar Mantar.“The proximity of the new Parliament premises has further enhanced the significance of regulating activities in the surrounding areas, having regard to the security and uninterrupted functioning of a vital constitutional institution."Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Who protects those counting America's votes? US election workers face threats amid midterms
articles.summary: Across the United States, local government workers responsible for handling votes in the midterm elections are facing tighter security measures amid
articles.body: Across the United States, local government workers responsible for handling votes in the midterm elections are facing tighter security measures amid concerns about physical threats, surveillance and harassment.After years of rising hostility towards election staff, local election offices have increased security at their buildings. Measures include bulletproof glass, restricted entry systems and emergency panic buttons connected to local law enforcement.In Maricopa County, Arizona, election officials have taken additional steps to protect counting facilities. Security preparations across the country also include training for election workers on handling threats, suspicious packages and aggressive behaviour.The risks facing election workers were highlighted in an October 29 report by WBUR's programme On Point with Meghna Chakrabarti. The report discussed threats ranging from suspicious packages containing unknown powders to drone surveillance, cyberattacks and attempts to disrupt election systems.Threats force shift in facility securityThe move to strengthen security at vote-counting centres comes after years of threats and intimidation against election personnel, particularly since the 2020 election.A 2025 survey by the Brennan Center for Justice found that 38 per cent of local election officials had experienced threats, harassment or abuse because of their work. The organisation's 2026 survey also found that 32 per cent of officials had faced such treatment, while 14 per cent reported being threatened.The October 29 WBUR report also examined how election officials are preparing for possible disruption. Tina Barton, co-chair of the Committee for Safe and Secure Elections, discussed concerns about drones, bomb threats, suspicious powder-filled packages and cyberattacks targeting election systems.According to WBUR, Barton said her organisation had conducted more than 140 training sessions for local government officials and law enforcement in 2026, more than double the number held in 2024.The scale of the problem has also affected election staffing. In a February 3 report, the non-partisan group Issue One found that 50 per cent of chief local election officials in Western states had left their positions between November 2020 and November 2025. More than 250 officials had left these roles across the 11 Western states examined.De-escalation training and panic buttonsApart from improving security at buildings, election departments are also focusing on protecting workers inside polling stations and vote-counting centres.In many areas, election officials are preparing staff to deal with aggressive behaviour and possible security incidents. Training includes recognising threats, handling confrontations and contacting emergency services.The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), part of the US Department of Homeland Security, has traditionally provided election officials with security guidance, information about threats and support for protecting election infrastructure.However, the Brennan Center's April 13, 2026 report on election officials found that cuts to federal election security support had raised concerns among local authorities. It also found that 86 per cent of surveyed officials considered election security training beneficial.Security measures also cover election technology and ballot transportation. Election officials use safeguards to protect voting equipment and maintain records of ballot handling. These steps are intended to protect the counting process and prevent interference.Intimidation drives staff shortages and legislative actionThreats and harassment have created another problem for local governments. Finding enough workers to manage polling stations on election day has become increasingly difficult.According to Issue One's February 2026 analysis, 50 per cent of chief local election officials in Western states had left their jobs over the five years following the 2020 presidential election. The organisation said roughly 76 per cent of the departures were voluntary.The Brennan Center's 2026 survey also found that more than half of local election officials were concerned that threats, harassment and intimidation could make it harder to recruit and retain election workers.To address these problems, several states have introduced legal protections for election officials. The Brennan Center's guide to laws against voter and election worker intimidation, published in June 2024, documents federal and state measures designed to protect people involved in elections from threats and harassment.Despite these protections, concerns about worker safety and recruitment remain.You use AI every day.
