articles.title: A British wildlife rescuer nursed a severely ill fox back to health; nine years later, she still seeks him out for a hug every day
articles.summary: Rescued fox Sweep and her wildlife rescuer Geoff Grewcock share a hug every single day at the Nuneaton and Warwickshire Wildlife Sanctuary in England,
articles.body: Rescued fox Sweep and her wildlife rescuer Geoff Grewcock share a hug every single day at the Nuneaton and Warwickshire Wildlife Sanctuary in England, nine years after the young vixen arrived very ill. Grewcock believes she had been poisoned, and he spent the following year nursing her back to health. She recovered fully, but she grew so attached to him that she could never be released into the wild. Today she lives alongside the other wild animals being rehabilitated at the rescue centre owned by Grewcock, who is in his seventies, and her deep affection for him has never faded.Why Sweep keeps demanding affection from Geoff Grewcock and what he believes her hugs really meanWild beim Wild reports that Grewcock describes Sweep as a lovable, friendly fox. Most visitors are allowed to stroke her, but she is closest to him and treats the daily cuddle as non-negotiable. In his view, it is her way of thanking the team for the care she has received.When Sweep first arrived, she was so lethargic and unwell that Grewcock feared there was little hope. He bottle-fed her for months and gave her saline solution by injection at night. Medication and plenty of cuddles followed, and she pulled through.What a London wildlife writer saw when the fox and her carer hugged for around ten minutesJames Cook, a 30-year-old wildlife content writer based in London, visited the sanctuary in June and saw the bond first-hand, Wild beim Wild reports. He said Sweep is “simply totally in love with Geoff”. The pair hugged for about ten minutes while he was there. Cook added that getting so close to a fox is rare, because foxes are not meant to be kept as pets.Inside the Nuneaton sanctuary, an animal lover has rescued over ninety thousand creaturesAccording to the sanctuary’s website, Grewcock was born in 1950 and spent 25 years as a cash-in-transit driver, until a serious accident at work ended his career. He used the damages he was awarded to fulfil a lifelong wish to care for animals. In February 2001, he began building the sanctuary, which later became a registered charity.By his seventieth birthday in 2020, the website says, he had rescued more than ninety thousand birds and animals and taught thousands of children and adults about wildlife care. He looks after the wildlife around the clock, with no days off and no pay. Volunteers and a registered veterinary surgeon support him, and a specially equipped wildlife ambulance lets the team rescue injured, sick and trapped animals and assist the emergency services. The Parliamentary Review also featured the sanctuary as a best-practice example in 2020.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Powys health board shake-up opposed as locals fight cuts to hospital beds
articles.summary: The plans would see inpatient beds reduced from 146 to either 90 or 60 in the county.
articles.body:
Proposals to cut community hospital beds in some of Wales' most rural areas have met with strong resistance.

The plans would see inpatient beds reduced from 146 to either 90 or 60 in Powys , with services concentrated in just two or three of the county's eight community hospitals.

It means inpatient wards could disappear from Welshpool, Machynlleth, Ystradgynlais and Llanidloes, while Llandrindod Wells could also lose its beds under the most extensive option.

Powys Teaching Health Board said the changes were needed to make services safe and sustainable, arguing that its current model was increasingly difficult to staff and deliver across such a large geographical area.

A 14-week public consultation on the future of health services in Powys was now under way, but the plans had already been opposed by GPs, politicians and communities concerned about the impact on an ageing rural population.

In August more than 400 people attended a public meeting in Llanidloes to oppose the closure of community hospital beds in the town.

A drop-in meeting was held in Llanidloes on Tuesday, following a number of public meetings in other parts of Powys to discuss the health board's plans.

Jill O'Connor, from the Llanidloes Hospital Alliance Group said plans to instead deliver more care in the community were not workable, arguing that it would be difficult to provide care for people who live at least 20 or 30 miles out of town in remote rural areas, particularly in the middle of winter.

"It beggars belief that they want to go and work, treat people in homes when actually... you can treat a bigger group collectively in a hospital rather than with individual staff," she said.

"And we don't think that they've actually put the infrastructure in place.

"Yes, they will have excess numbers of nurses... from the hospitals that they're going to close, but those people need training up," she said.

"The community feels very passionately that this is their hospital and it serves the community."

Powys has one of the oldest populations in Wales, with more than a quarter of residents aged over 65.

The health board estimates the average journey time to inpatient care could rise from around 12 minutes to 24 minutes under the proposals. For some people living furthest from hospitals, journeys could take more than 45 minutes each way.

The impact of potentially losing local inpatient facilities is causing concern for many families.

Tuppin Scrase said his wife died five years ago after receiving palliative care in Llanidloes, and that he would not have been able to see her if she had not been cared for further away.

"At that time, it was the time of Covid, and if she'd had to remain in Shrewsbury or Aberystwyth, which are our nearest general hospitals, I could never have seen her," he said.

"In the whole month it took her to die, I would not have been able to see her. It was only because it was local that I could actually get there and be with her."

Under its Better Together programme the health board is proposing changes to services in a range of areas - adult physical health, adult mental health, urgent care and some diagnostic services.

Among the proposed changes , the most controversial could affect inpatient beds in most of Powys' community hospitals where occupancy rates are usually around 85 to 90%.

Powys does not have a general hospital, but it does have beds in eight community hospitals.

According to a report to the health board the current model "provides valued local services, but its dispersed configuration makes it increasingly difficult to meet needs consistently".

It will consult on two possible options:

The first option would see beds located in three community hospitals in Brecon, Newtown and Llandrindod Wells. This would mean a reduction from 146 to around 90 inpatient beds for the whole of Powys.

The second option would see beds located in two community hospitals in Brecon and Newtown. This would mean a reduction to around 60 inpatient beds.

Any changes would happen over a number of years.

A health board report said about 40% of its budget is spent on services commissioned from outside of Powys - in the last financial year this was around £198m.

There are also proposed changes to Powys' minor injuries units and the way urgent care is delivered in the county.

At the moment, urgent care is delivered in a variety of ways including by GPs, an out of hours service, pharmacies and health board minor injuries units.

But the health board believes the current service "does not provide consistent or equitable access across the county" and demand for urgent care is increasing.

Its is proposing two options for changes to urgent care and diagnostic services.

The first option would see urgent care available on three sites - Urgent Care Centres (UCCs) would be established in Newtown and Brecon, and a minor injuries unit in Llandrindod Wells, operating from eight in the morning until eight at night, seven days a week.

The minor injury unit would stay in Welshpool until the UCC opens in Newtown, and then the minor injury unit in Welshpool would close.

The second option would see just two UCCs in Newtown and Brecon.

One option for changes to mental health services is proposed - the consolidation of all adult and older adult mental health services at a single site, either at Bronllys hospital or a new site in the Bronllys/Brecon area, as well as expanding community mental health services.

The health board said their proposals responded to major challenges facing health services.

"People are living longer, often with several long-term conditions; demand is rising; and recruiting and retaining the workforce needed to sustain small services across a large rural county is becoming increasingly difficult," Powys Teaching Health Board said in a statement previously.

It said the overhaul was necessary to ensure services could "remain safe, effective and sustainable, while helping more people stay well, remain independent and receive care at home or closer to home".

The consultation closes on 10 January 2027.

articles.title: Asmongold blasts Dead by Daylight over TheBurntPeanut backlash, calls developer’s response ‘pathetic capitulation’
articles.summary: Zack “Asmongold” has criticized Dead by Daylight’s latest response to the backlash over TheBurntPeanut receiving free game content.
articles.body: Zack “Asmongold” has criticized Dead by Daylight’s latest response to the backlash over TheBurntPeanut receiving free game content. The streamer called the developer’s move a “pathetic capitulation that will earn the respect of no one.” His comment came after Behaviour Interactive confirmed that it had taken back the rewards and was reviewing how its team works with creators. The dispute began during a Halloween livestream on October 30, when TheBurntPeanut was given access to game content, leading players to question the decision and the studio’s response. Some players also questioned his past comments on stream.Zack “Asmongold” criticizes Dead by Daylight over its response to TheBurntPeanutAsmongold shared his reaction on X after Behaviour Interactive published a detailed follow-up. He accused the developer of giving in to people who had allegedly harassed and doxxed one of its employees. His post read:“Groveling and begging for the approval of mentally ill gender confused freaks after they doxxed and harassed one of your employees. Pathetic capitulation that will earn the respect of no one”The claims about doxxing and harassment are part of Asmongold’s post and should not be taken as proof that everyone who criticized the game was involved.The dispute began on October 30, when TheBurntPeanut played Dead by Daylight during a Halloween stream with other creators. He found that the game’s team had given his account access to characters, skins and other content. The official game account also joined the chat. When the streamer offered to return the items, a team member replied, “WE CAN TAKE THE HEAT!”Some players questioned why he had received the content and pointed to comments he had made in the past. TheBurntPeanut later denied that his streams showed he was racist or transphobic.Dead by Daylight explains TheBurntPeanut giveaway and confirms the content was removedBehaviour Interactive first addressed the issue on November 1. It said the team member had given TheBurntPeanut content and currency without the required approval. The developer also said the employee’s later comments did not match the game’s values and apologized to players.In its four-part follow-up on November 2, Behaviour said staff had noticed a very large audience watching the game’s Twitch category and wanted to welcome new players. However, the decision to give TheBurntPeanut the content and join his chat was made too quickly and without the usual team discussion.The studio said it normally checks a new creator’s past content to see whether it fits the inclusive community it wants to build. That review did not happen properly in this case. Behaviour also admitted that its internal rules did not have enough checks to stop a team member from giving away items without wider approval.The developer said the “WE CAN TAKE THE HEAT!” reply ignored the situation and crossed the line for an official brand account. It added that the message made things worse for the community, including creators who had to deal with the fallout.Behaviour confirmed that it had removed the content from TheBurntPeanut’s account. It also plans to update its creator rules and approval process. Creators found to have broken the Creator Program Policy could be removed. The studio said it was taking internal action but would not share details because the matter was confidential.The policy bars creators in the program from taking part in bullying, harassment, hate speech, transphobia and other harmful conduct. Shani’s tenth aspect also falls on Sagittarius, your fourth house of home and vehicles. If there’s a home loan or a car loan in the family, pull out the papers and check the rate and the remaining tenure. Charges you never noticed may be sitting in there.The Small Dues Add UpRahu sits in Aquarius, your sixth house, and it’s good at hiding small debts behind bigger ones. Pay-later apps are the usual culprits. An unpaid electricity bill with a late fee attached is another. A quick search of your inbox for the word “reminder” might tell you more than you expect.Keep the Wallet Closed TonightThe Moon is in Purva Phalguni in Leo, your twelfth house, along with Jupiter and Ketu. Comfort spending will look tempting, whether that’s a weekend booking or a new gadget. Jupiter here does support giving, and a small donation is fine. articles.title: Judge needn't face strictures for typos in judgement: SC
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Some factual errors in a judgement delivered by her, allegedly due to a 'cut, copy and paste' job, had cost a trial judge dear, resulting in
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Some factual errors in a judgement delivered by her, allegedly due to a 'cut, copy and paste' job, had cost a trial judge dear, resulting in Rajasthan HC castigating her and sending her to a judicial academy for training. But Supreme Court has come to the judge's rescue and struck off the adverse observations against her, holding that criticising a judicial officer for inadvertent typographical errors in a judgement, which did not affect the outcome of the case, was unwarranted.A bench of Justices Sandeep Mehta and Devendra Kumar Upadhyaya allowed the plea of the judge and expunged the strictures and adverse remarks against her."Ex facie, we feel that the adverse observations and the strictures recorded by HC against the judicial officer were uncalled for and avoidable. These disparaging remarks and the strictures were recorded on the judicial side without affording an opportunity to the judicial officer to show-cause or to place her explanation on record before such observations and strictures were made, and hence, suffer from the vice of nonadherence to the principles of natural justice," it said.HC observed the judicial officer "had used the methodology of 'cut, copy and paste' and in all probability, the judgement had been scripted by the stenographer/clerk concerned and was signed without being read and corrected by the presiding officer as she failed to strike out the irrelevant paragraphs which related to the trial of the adult accused".The trial judge had passed two judgements arising out of the same case as one of the accused was a minor. After appreciating the evidence in both trials, the judicial officer pronounced separate judgements convicting both the accused of the charges against them and sentencing each to 20 years' RI.SC said it seemed that during the course of rendering judgements in the two cases, some extracts of evidence/numerical details from one trial were inadvertently incorporated into the judgement for the other.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A Pennsylvania woman was treated for breast cancer before doctors discovered a rare lymphoma; after her death, the family's malpractice case was dismissed, but the state's highest court has cleared it for a jury
articles.summary: A Pennsylvania woman who underwent treatment for breast cancer for more than a year was later found to have a rare and aggressive form of lymphoma.
articles.body: A Pennsylvania woman who underwent treatment for breast cancer for more than a year was later found to have a rare and aggressive form of lymphoma. Tanya Smith died in January 2019, and her family pursued a medical malpractice lawsuit, alleging that doctors had failed to investigate conflicting test results and delayed her correct treatment. The case was dismissed during a jury trial, but on October 29, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court upheld a ruling allowing the family's claims to be heard by a jury.The dispute began in March 2017, when Smith visited an oncological surgeon at WellSpan York Hospital after an enlarged lymph node was discovered in her armpit during treatment for shoulder pain, as per the case details on Justia. A biopsy was performed, and pathologist Dr John Wright reported findings compatible with metastatic breast cancer, suggesting that cancer originating in the breast had spread to the lymph node.However, further examinations raised questions about that diagnosis. A CT scan, PET scan, mammogram and ultrasound failed to identify a primary tumour or show that the cancer had originated in the breast. The CT and PET scans also listed lymphoma as a possible diagnosis. Despite these findings, Smith began treatment for breast cancer under oncologist Dr Annie Kannarkatt at Cancer Care Associates of York on March 21, 2017.The treatment included chemotherapy and radiation therapy. Although the areas receiving radiation showed improvement, chemotherapy produced little or no improvement in her overall condition. By November 2017, another PET scan showed that the cancer had spread considerably. The disease later affected her abdomen, leading to the removal of her gallbladder in March 2018.Doctors discover rare lymphoma A biopsy of cancerous tissue removed during Smith's gallbladder surgery changed the course of her diagnosis. Doctors identified ALK-positive large B-cell lymphoma, an extremely rare and aggressive cancer.When the medical team re-examined tissue collected in March 2017, it matched the samples obtained a year later. This established that Smith had been suffering from lymphoma from the beginning, rather than metastatic breast cancer.Following the revised diagnosis, Smith transferred to Milton S. Hershey Medical Center, where oncologist Dr Seema Naik began lymphoma-directed chemotherapy. The initial treatment produced little improvement.Doctors then administered salvage chemotherapy, which reduced the amount of cancer enough for Smith to undergo a stem cell transplant. However, the transplant was unsuccessful, and her cancer returned. She died on January 6, 2019.Before her death, Smith and her husband, Marvin Smith, had filed a lawsuit against Kannarkatt and Cancer Care Associates. They alleged that the oncologist had failed to confirm the original diagnosis, consult the pathology team about conflicting findings and provide appropriate chemotherapy.Could earlier treatment have improved chances?During the proceedings, medical experts examined whether the delay had reduced Smith's chances of surviving longer.Dr Gerald Goldklang, an expert called by the family, explained that oncologists must consider pathology results alongside clinical examinations and imaging tests. He testified that Kannarkatt should have questioned the initial diagnosis because subsequent investigations did not support breast cancer.Another expert, Dr Robert Soiffer, explained that ALK-positive large B-cell lymphoma was particularly difficult to treat because of its aggressive nature and rarity.He testified that cancers receiving inadequate treatment can continue growing, develop mutations and become resistant to chemotherapy. Earlier lymphoma-directed treatment, he said, could have offered Smith a better opportunity for remission and a successful transplant.Asked whether the 13-month delay had deprived Smith of a substantially better chance of living longer, Soiffer replied, “I think it did, yes.”However, he acknowledged that he could not predict exactly how long Smith would have survived with earlier treatment.SC says jury must decide malpractice claimThe family's first trial in October 2021 ended without a verdict because the jury could not agree. During a second trial in April 2022, the judge dismissed the case after concluding that the family had not presented sufficient evidence linking the alleged negligence to Smith's harm.A Pennsylvania appeals court overturned that decision in March 2024 and ordered a new trial. Kannarkatt and Cancer Care Associates challenged the ruling before the state's Supreme Court.In its October 29 judgment, the Supreme Court agreed that the family's evidence was sufficient for a jury to consider whether the alleged failure to investigate the diagnosis increased Smith's risk of harm.The court explained that medical malpractice cases involving delayed treatment do not always require proof that a patient would certainly have survived with different care. Expert evidence showing that alleged negligence increased the risk of harm can be sufficient to allow a jury to decide the matter.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'My approval rating there is 99%': Trump jokes he'll move to Israel and become PM if Americans get 'tired' of him
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has joked about moving to Israel and becoming its prime minister if Americans ever get tired of him, making the remark during a
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has joked about moving to Israel and becoming its prime minister if Americans ever get tired of him, making the remark during a Fox News interview on Election Day.Speaking to Fox News on Tuesday, the POTUS claimed he had a 99 per cent approval rating in Israel and suggested he could pursue a political career there if his popularity in the United States declined."In fact, if people ever got tired of me in the US, I'll move to Israel, become prime minister," Trump said.According to TMZ, Trump made the remark while discussing the relationship between the United States and Israel. He also claimed to have the "highest approval rating of anybody in history", but did not provide any polling evidence to support the statement.His reported popularity in Israel stands in contrast to his approval rating at home. TMZ reported that Trump's US approval rating was 32 per cent, although it did not identify the poll behind the figure.Trump praises Israel, announces end to US aidDuring the Fox News interview, Trump also praised Israel as an important American ally and spoke about his administration's actions against Iran.He announced that US would stop providing around $4 billion in annual assistance to Israel by the end of 2026. Fox News reported that Trump said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had raised the idea of ending the assistance and that the two leaders had discussed it for several years.Trump argued that Israel no longer needed the financial support because of its economic strength. However, the announcement raises questions about the future of the existing US-Israel military assistance agreement, which provides around $3.8 billion annually through 2028, according to Fox News.Trump had made a similar remark earlierThis is not the first time Trump has joked about becoming Israel's prime minister. According to TMZ, he made a similar remark in May, when he also claimed to enjoy 99 per cent support among Israelis.His latest comments came as Americans voted in the 2026 midterm elections on November 3. The elections will determine which party controls the US Congress, including the House of Representatives and the Senate.Trump's Republicans are defending their congressional majorities against the opposition Democrats. The results could shape the remainder of his presidency, including his domestic and foreign policy agenda.The 2026 US midterm elections will determine control of all 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 Senate seats. Republicans are entering the elections with a narrow 219-214 advantage in the House, while holding 53 of the Senate's 100 seats. Democrats need to gain just four net seats in the House and four in the Senate to take control of both chambers. The party that wins the House needs at least 218 seats, while a Senate majority requires 51 seats, or 50 if the vice-president can break a tie. The elections are crucial for Trump, as a Democratic takeover of either chamber could make it harder for him to pass legislation, while giving the opposition greater power to investigate his administration and challenge his policies.You use AI every day. articles.title: Code cracked for Margam shipwreck padlock solving 400-year-old mystery
articles.summary: The brass lock, found in the sand near Port Talbot, forms part of a 1583 shipwreck treasure hoard.
articles.body:
Experts have cracked a four-letter code to open an ancient padlock from a shipwreck off the Welsh coast using modern scanning technology.

The 400-year-old brass lock was discovered by metal detectorist Peter Hughes in the sand near Margam in Port Talbot, in 1999.

It forms part of a wider treasure hoard from the Ann Francis ship that was caught in a storm on 28 December 1583 on the way back from Spain. Its cargo was hidden beneath the sand for centuries.

Museum experts have used CT scanning to examine the lock's internal mechanism, identify the correct letter combination and solve the mystery.

Peter Hughes, from Maesteg, said the padlock was one of hundreds of artefacts he found after decades of searching on Morfa beach.

Found near a collection of Spanish silver coins and close to two coin weights, it is thought the lock may have protected these objects or secured a chest containing valuable items that did not survive, like documents or textiles.

"It was by chance - a day off. I was walking along the beach with my metal detector on a day off, and I came across a coin," the 69-year-old said.

"That was the start of a journey that lasted 21 years."

He said he was "delighted" that the expert team at Amgueddfa Cymru and Cardiff University cracked the padlock code after he spent years trying to solve the mystery himself.

"I tried to unlock it for about 20 years, I tried moving the dials, finding the right combinations, and I failed," he said.

"But with the aid of modern technology we've been able to crack what's like the Da Vinci code, really.

"For me, it's like opening the Ark of the Covenant, and I'm delighted, truly thrilled."

Dr David Williams, a research associate based at Cardiff University's School of Engineering, said he was "sceptical" when he was asked to use a scanning device to try and solve the mystery.

"It's challenging, the device we have is not designed to this particular purpose," he said.

"This is micro CT scanning, something you'd get at the hospital, but for smaller items."

Williams said he was "always open to a challenge" and trying to "figure out a puzzle".

"We did a first scan to see if we could see anything and we were quite surprised that we could see letters," he said.

"The second scan went terribly, but with the third scan, we tried a different approach, and figured out the code.

"I was blown away that we actually cracked it."

Hughes passed on the hoard of artefacts to Amgueddfa Cymru in 2017, and the collection, with the lock in the centre, was put on display at Swansea Waterfront Museum in July 2026 .

Senior curator Alastair Willis said the discovery of the code, which spells out ANCE, was "incredible".

"It's really complex because there are so many combinations," he said.

"There are four different rings, and because there are six different letters on each of the rings, there are 1,296 different combinations, and you have to make sure they're aligned with the loop at the top."

His colleague at Amgueddfa Cymru, senior curator Siân Iles, said the lock was in "excellent condition" and paints a picture of the period.

"This is a wonderful example of one that still functions as it would have done hundreds of years ago," she said.

"Because it was found so close to the wreck of the Ann Francis and with all the material that's part of that collection, it provides a really good context, it allows us to really tightly date it.

"I've seen others, and they're usually corroded and in different parts, but it was in wonderful condition.

"It's a small object so it probably would have been a lock for a chest or a small box, we don't know the content, and that's part of the story, there are some things we'll never know, but it's something that would have meant something to the person who knew that code."

What should you do if you discover treasure?

Treasure has a variety of definitions , as per the Treasure Act of 1996.

In Wales, if you find treasure it must be reported to a Finds Liaison Officer within 14 days of first finding it or within 14 days of realising an item might be treasure, even if you have had it for longer.

Only items officially defined as treasure need to be reported and there is a fine or up to three months in prison for not reporting.

There are different rules for Scotland and Northern Ireland .

After a find is reported, you will be contacted by either a Finds Liaison Officer or museum curator to talk about how and where you made the find.

The Finds Liaison Officer or museum curator will then write a report on the find and the coroner will hold an inquest.

The Finds Liaison Officer will help you get the coins assessed by experts to determine if they meet the legal definition of "treasure" under the Treasure Act 1996 .

If a museum wants the treasure, the Treasure Valuation Committee will ask an expert to value the find.

They will recommend to the Secretary of State for the Department for Culture, Media and Sport how much the treasure is worth and how much should go to anyone eligible for a share of a reward.
